historical_timeline.summary: Born at Pella in Macedonia, the son of King Philip II and Olympias.
Battle wounds: a blow to the head at the Granicus, a sword wound to the thigh at Issus, a catapult bolt into the shoulder at Gaza.
Grave illness with fever and convulsions in Cilicia after bathing in the cold river Cydnus; recovers.
Kills his officer Clitus at a drinking party.
Near-fatal arrow wound of the chest at a town of the Malli; recovers slowly.
His closest companion, Hephaestion, dies of a fever at Ecbatana; his grief is great.
Winter campaign against the Cossaeans; marches back to Babylon in the spring.
Dies at Babylon at 32 after a fever of about two weeks; the cause is unknown and disputed. Whether he had a drinking disorder is disputed.

claims.statement: Ancient historians record many battle wounds: a sword wound to the thigh at Issus, a catapult bolt through shield and breastplate into the shoulder at Gaza, from which he 'was not easily cured', and a blow to the head at the Granicus. In a speech that Arrian writes for him, he says that no part of the front of his body is free from wounds.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented history of repeated combat injury; no lasting effect is used in the modern episode except the chest wound (CLM-0003).

claims.statement: Storming a town of the Malli in the Indus valley (326 or 325 BC), he was shot with an arrow under the breast through his breastplate into the chest; Arrian cites Ptolemy that air was breathed out from the wound with the blood. He fainted from loss of blood, the arrowhead lodged at a rib was cut out, he swooned again at its removal, and Plutarch says it brought him to death's door, but he recovered after a long time under regimen and treatment.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern chest wall pain and pleural thickening; the modern findings are synthetic and are not a claim about his real chest.

claims.statement: The ancient historians describe long drinking parties with his Companions, especially in his later years, and disagreed about how much he drank: Aristobulus, quoted by Arrian, held that he 'was not a great wine-drinker' and sat long over wine for companionship, and Plutarch that he was 'less addicted to wine than was generally believed'; Plutarch also tells of a contest in drinking unmixed wine after which the winner and many others died.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented reports of heavy drinking at banquets, with the ancient disagreement kept; they anchor the modern drinking pattern but make no diagnosis for him.

claims.statement: Whether he had what would now be called an alcohol use disorder is disputed. A psychiatric review of the ancient historians concluded that he periodically drank large quantities of undiluted wine to the point of pathological intoxication, but that the data do not give convincing evidence of abuse or dependence by DSM-IV or ICD-10 criteria, and that alcohol was unlikely to have caused his death; a medical historian has questioned retrospective diagnoses of this kind.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and disputed; the modern alcohol use disorder is synthetic and is mild, not a claim about his real drinking.

claims.statement: In October 324 BC at Ecbatana, during games and drinking parties, his closest companion Hephaestion fell sick with a fever and died on about the seventh day. The historians agree that his grief was great: until the third day he neither ate nor cared for his appearance, and the mourning lasted many days. Accounts that he hanged or crucified the physician differ.

claims.statement: The cause of his death is unknown and much argued. Modern proposals include typhoid fever (an NEJM clinicopathological discussion and a review that found the court journal's account most characteristic of typhoid), malaria, West Nile virus encephalitis, poisoning (Veratrum album thought the most plausible poison if he was poisoned), alcohol, and Guillain-Barre syndrome with a false diagnosis of death; each has been disputed. Plutarch thought the story of poisoning a fabrication.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and disputed; the record takes no side, and nothing about the cause of his death is used or foreshadowed in the modern episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Chest wall pain and reduced lung function after a penetrating chest injury, with heavy episodic drinking and grief, in a young commander on campaign: a 32-year-old who was shot through the left chest some years ago comes in with pain at the scar and breathlessness on long marches, and is found to drink heavily at banquets since the death of his closest companion five months ago. The episode covers the chest X-ray and spirometry, with a reduced FVC and a normal ratio that needs lung volumes (ATS/ERS 2019 and the ERS/ATS 2022 interpretation standard); CT for a retained fragment, pleural thickening and a trapped lung; why a localized fibrothorax with mild restriction is not an indication for decortication (BTS 2023); non-opioid treatment of post-traumatic intercostal pain (acetaminophen with a lower limit, a lidocaine patch, physical therapy, and an intercostal nerve block if needed), avoiding opioids and sedating medicines while he drinks (CDC 2022); the AUDIT, the DSM-5-TR criteria and PEth, a mild alcohol use disorder and a moderation goal chosen with him, with medicine offered (APA 2018, VA/DoD 2021, USPSTF 2018); grief that is not yet prolonged grief disorder and is not major depression, followed with the PHQ-9; the safety assessment and lethal-means counseling; travel and campaign health in Mesopotamia (no malaria chemoprophylaxis where there is no transmission, bite precautions, typhoid and hepatitis A vaccines, and tetanus for a wound); and a plan that keeps him fit to lead.

Since then an ache at the scar that is sharp on deep breaths, climbs and lifting, 6 of 10, and breathlessness on long climbs that is slowly worse; no cough, sputum, blood, fevers or weight loss. Older wounds of the head, shoulder and thigh; a grave febrile illness in his early twenties, recovered. Never smoked. Drinks ten or more drinks of wine at banquets two or three nights a week, more since the death of his closest companion five months ago; no morning drinking or withdrawal; AUDIT 19; PEth 236 ng/mL. PHQ-9 12 with item 9 scored 0; a safety assessment found no current risk; safety plan and the 988 line given. Examination: blood pressure 134/84, pulse 82, oxygen saturation 98 percent, BMI 25.1; slightly reduced expansion and breath sounds at the left base; a healed scar in the left fourth intercostal space with tenderness along the fifth rib. Chest X-ray today: left lateral and posterior pleural thickening with a blunted costophrenic angle, a healed left fifth rib fracture, no foreign body or pneumothorax. Spirometry today: FVC 3.92 L (78 percent), FEV1 3.29 L (79 percent), ratio 0.84. Liver tests: AST 52, ALT 41, GGT 96 U/L. Medicines: acetaminophen up to 2,000 mg a day, thiamine 100 mg daily. consultant_note.history: Thank you for asking me to see Alexander, a 32-year-old army commander, for chest wall pain and breathlessness years after a penetrating arrow wound of the left chest. The history is as in your letter. The pain is localized to the scar and the rib below it, is sharp on deep breaths and twisting, and wakes him when he lies on his left side; it has never been pressing or brought on by effort alone. The breathlessness comes on at the top of long climbs and with heavy kit and settles within minutes. He has had no cough, sputum, blood, fevers, night sweats, wheeze or chest infections since the wound. He has never smoked and has no workplace dust exposure. He drank less at two banquets this fortnight and saw the addiction medicine clinician this morning.
